summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Cobalt Retail through Console tracing, error analysis, and request logs. Focus on debugging flows: how to correlate traces to request IDs, filter by route/model, and export logs for root-cause. Customer concerns: PII redaction, audit logs, SSO and data residency. Agreed next steps: share SOC2 package, export sample traces, run pilot benchmarks.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-11-30
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood Solutions); Jake Martinez (Cobalt Head of ML), Sara Liu (Platform Eng), Arjun Mehta (SRE), Emily Park (PM)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll hand off to Liam for the demo in a sec. Quick recap of agenda — tracing, error analysis, request logs, and a short debugging flow.
[00:20] Jake Martinez: Thanks, Maya. We're most interested in how quickly we can find root cause when a generation starts returning hallucinations or a tokenization error pops up.
[00:35] Liam O'Neill: Totally, we'll show the trace view, how traces map to request IDs, and then request logs. I'll start screen share, bear with me while I pull up the console.
[01:05] [screen share noise] Liam O'Neill: Alright, so this is the Redwood Console. Top-left you can see Routes, Models, the Tracing tab. We often see customers start with the Requests list — it includes the request id, model, route, latency, tokens, and an error column if present.
[01:30] Sara Liu: Quick q — can we filter by customer tenant or api key? We have multiple teams in one account.
[01:40] Liam O'Neill: Yes, you can filter by API key or agent id; we also show metadata tags you can add on each request to correlate. Small caveat: labels sometimes come through in the payload and need to be consistent.
[02:05] Arjun Mehta: And retention? We keep logs for 90 days but for debugging we may need longer export.
[02:12] Maya Chen: We can export on-demand — there are retention addons, we discussed those in the SOC2 package — we'll include options for extended log storage.
[02:30] Liam O'Neill: Back to tracing — here's a trace for a recent failing request. Notice the root span is the request, then we have sub-spans for tokenization, model inference, kv-cache lookups and post-processing. If there's an error it's surfaced on the span where it happened.
[02:55] [ambient noise] Liam O'Neill: Example — see this span flagged red? That's a decoding error in the model runtime. Clicking it surfaces the stack snippet and the request payload metadata, including prompt and prompt length.
[03:25] Emily Park: Are prompts visible in the trace by default? We need to know about PII concerns.
[03:34] Liam O'Neill: Great question. By default prompts are stored and visible to users in the same org. For extra privacy you can enable prompt redaction at ingest — either full redaction or token-level hashing. We can show the toggle.
[03:55] Jake Martinez: We need KMS-backed encryption and proof of deletion for compliance — any notes?
[04:05] Maya Chen: We integrate with customer-managed KMS for Private deployments. For hosted accounts we provide envelope encryption and audit logs. I'll attach the KMS section from our security doc after the call.
[04:22] Liam O'Neill: Now filtering — you can search traces by request id, route name, model name, status code, and even by span attribute. Typo sometimes in the console search — it autocompletes but can mismatch model names from on-prem models.
[04:45] [01:00 minute mark] Liam O'Neill: Walkthrough: we find an erroneous request ID in the requests list, click to open trace, then correlate to the request log entry which has raw request/response, headers, and timing.
[05:10] Sara Liu: Do request logs include response tokens? We don't want full responses stored for certain models.
[05:18] Liam O'Neill: You can set response retention and redaction at route level. Also we support partial response logging: store only token counts and error indicators instead of full text.
[05:35] Arjun Mehta: Show us a live example where a rate-limit caused a cascade failure.
[05:40] Liam O'Neill: Sure — I have a synthetic trace. Here, span shows throttling on the serving layer, then a fallback to a smaller model — you'll see the route-level policy triggered a fallback. The trace lets you see the timing: batch wait time increased before fallback.
[06:20] Jake Martinez: That fallback behavior is important — can we control fallback thresholds?
[06:25] Liam O'Neill: Yep — there's a policy config in the routes page. Thresholds, allowed fallback models, and auto-retry cadence.
[06:40] [06:30 mark] Liam O'Neill: Next, request logs viewer — it's essentially a searchable raw log with structured fields. You can export as ndjson or csv, or push to S3. Here's export dropdown.
[07:05] Emily Park: Are exported logs scrubbed automatically? We want a clean export for auditors.
[07:12] Liam O'Neill: Exports respect your redaction settings. If redaction is enabled, sensitive fields are masked in the export. Otherwise you get full payloads.
[07:30] Jake Martinez: For the pilot we want to share a few failing traces; what's the best way?
[07:38] Liam O'Neill: Best practice: create a temporary access role with limited permissions, generate an export for the specific request ids, and upload to a shared S3 or secure link. I'll prepare a sample export with anonymized prompts.
[07:55] [07:50] Priya Rao: Also pointing out the trace-events API — you can pull traces programmatically for your own observability stack. Note: export rates are throttled to protect multi-tenant performance.
[08:12] Jake Martinez: We'll want to ingest into our ELK for correlation. Any schema docs?
[08:18] Liam O'Neill: Yes, schema link is in the docs; I'll drop it in the follow-up.
[08:30] [08:25] Liam O'Neill: Now error analysis panel — this aggregates errors by type (decode_error, rate_limit, model_error, timeouts). You can open an error group to see top request examples and stack traces.
[08:55] Sara Liu: Does it do anomaly detection for sudden spikes?
[09:00] Liam O'Neill: We have basic anomaly alerts based on baselines, and a more advanced signals pack in Redwood Optimize (separate module) for drift/regression detection.
[09:18] Jake Martinez: Any guidance on mapping errors to changes in prompt engineering versus infra issues?
[09:25] Liam O'Neill: The tool surfaces span-level metrics. If tokenization fails before model span, it's likely prompt or tokenizer. If inference timeouts and there's high batch wait, it's infra. We demo both.
[09:45] [10:00] Liam O'Neill: Quick live filter: status:500 AND model:gptx-1 AND span:decode -> shows about 6 requests in last 24 hours. Click one.
[10:10] [crosstalk] Jake Martinez: I see the payload on the right, but the grammar is weird — that's probably a transcription mismatch in the console link.
[10:25] Liam O'Neill: Yeah sometimes generated text includes unicode characters that the console escapes oddly. We can export raw JSON to validate.
[10:45] Emily Park: How do we correlate traces to backend logs (kube/pods)?
[10:52] Liam O'Neill: Each trace has a host span attribute with instance id and pod id. You can map that to your infra logs if you're running Redwood Private or Dedicated and have logging hooks. For hosted, we provide linkable host ids and a short-lived snapshot for debugging.
[11:20] Arjun Mehta: For on-prem deployment, are the traces stored in customer infra?
[11:26] Maya Chen: Yes, for Private deployments the control plane is customer-managed and traces/logs stay in your VPC. We'll include that in the security doc.
[11:40] [11:30] Liam O'Neill: Next demo — root cause: tokenization mismatch. Here, model expects byte-pair tokens, we saw a mismatch because the client used a different encoding. The trace shows tokenization span throwing non-utf8 char warning.
[12:05] Sara Liu: Can we set alerts on those specific spans?
[12:10] Liam O'Neill: Yes, we let you create span-level monitors that feed into PagerDuty/Slack.
[12:25] Jake Martinez: Ok show us request-log export flow.
[12:30] Liam O'Neill: From a request view click Export -> choose ndjson -> pick fields (timestamp, request_id, route, model, response_status, prompt_hash, tokens_count) -> include payload? you can toggle. I'll create a sample export now.
[13:05] [keyboard typing] Liam O'Neill: Export done — link: https://shared.redwood/sample-exports/cobalt-anon-traces.ndjson (note: this is a placeholder link for demo).
[13:25] Emily Park: Good. Can we automate exports for all error-type=decode every day?
[13:32] Liam O'Neill: We have scheduled exports in the console; can run daily with filters and push to your S3. There's also a webhook for real-time pushing when errors occur.
[13:48] [14:00] Priya Rao: A small note: there are edge cases where auto-redaction might remove tokens we actually need for debugging. We support field-level redaction lists so you can keep certain fields.
[14:15] Sara Liu: For our PCI/team rules we need only token counts and anonymized prompts — can we configure at the route level?
[14:22] Maya Chen: Yes that's a route-level configuration. We'll include example JSON policy in the follow-up.
[14:35] [15:00] Liam O'Neill: Now let's walk a debugging flow end-to-end: customer raises ticket with request id -> SRE uses trace to see span timings -> correlates to request log for payload -> checks error group for similar occurrences -> runs a test with same prompt in sandbox route -> if infra related, enable fallback or scale pool -> if prompt-related, update prompt or model.
[15:30] Jake Martinez: How much access do your AE/SEs have to logs during pilot?
[15:36] Maya Chen: Only what's explicitly shared; we'll set up a temporary auditor role for troubleshooting. Redwood engineers don't access customer data without role-based invite.
[15:50] Arjun Mehta: Is there an audit trail of who viewed which traces?
[15:55] Liam O'Neill: Yes, the Console records trace access as part of audit logs with user, timestamp and action.
[16:10] [16:00 mark] Emily Park: Any latency impact of tracing on inference?
[16:15] Liam O'Neill: Tracing is asynchronous by default; span collection adds minimal overhead (<5ms typical). We can turn sampling rates down in high throughput routes.
[16:35] Jake Martinez: What about costs? Storing full traces for millions of requests seems expensive.
[16:40] Liam O'Neill: Agreed. We recommend sampling for production, full trace retention for error-heavy routes, and aggregated metrics for long-term. Redwood Optimize can surface cost-benefit for sampling rates.
[17:05] [17:00] Liam O'Neill: Demoing the trace compare feature — useful when rolling a model version. It overlays p50/p95 token latency and error rate between two releases.
[17:25] Sara Liu: That will help with our rollout plan.
[17:30] Jake Martinez: Regarding SSO, we use Okta. Is SAML supported?
[17:35] Maya Chen: Yes, SAML SSO + SCIM for provisioning is supported. We'll attach SSO docs.
[17:45] Emily Park: Anything around data residency? We need EU-only storage for some routes.
[17:50] Liam O'Neill: We support region pinning for routes and can restrict storage to a region for hosted customers. For strict residency, Private deployment in your cloud region is typical.
[18:05] [18:00] Liam O'Neill: Quick note on debugging: when you export traces, each entry includes a prompt_hash — use that to match across stores without exposing raw text.
[18:20] Arjun Mehta: Ok show the sample trace export contents.
[18:25] [keyboard] Liam O'Neill: Export snippet: {"timestamp":"2026-11-29T04:22:11Z","request_id":"r-0a1b2c","prompt_hash":"h_xxx","route":"prod-chat","model":"rdr-gpt-lite","status":"error","error_type":"decode_error","tokens":142} — that's the ndjson line.
[18:55] Jake Martinez: Perfect. We'll need those docs and the masked export for our auditors.
[19:05] Maya Chen: We'll send SOC2 + KMS + SSO docs.
[19:12] Liam O'Neill: Last part — debugging with request logs and infra correlation. You can attach pod logs and core dumps to a trace in Private/Dedicated. In hosted we provide ephemeral snapshots that expire after 7 days.
[19:40] Emily Park: How do we escalate? We want a P1 runbook.
[19:45] Maya Chen: Enterprise tier includes 4hr response SLAs and a P1 runbook. We'll share the runbook examples.
[19:58] [20:00] Jake Martinez: One more ops question — can we throttle debug export API so our team doesn't accidentally pull terabytes?
[20:05] Liam O'Neill: Yes, export API has quotas per account and can be limited via policy.
[20:20] [20:15] Priya Rao: I'll call out a known caveat: sometimes model names in traces are shortened in older exports which causes search mismatch; it's a UI bug slated for Q1 fix.
[20:40] Sara Liu: Any competitors do this differently?
[20:45] Maya Chen: Some provide logs only, not full trace spans. Others lock you into their deployment type; Redwood aims to be consistent across Hosted/Dedicated/Private.
[21:05] [21:00] Liam O'Neill: Quick recap and demo highlights — how to go from request to trace to log to export, redaction knobs, scheduled exports, and span-level alerts.
[21:30] Jake Martinez: Sounds good. Next steps?
[21:35] Maya Chen: Action items: we'll send SOC2 & SSO docs, Liam will prepare anonymized sample exports, Jake will share failing request ids by Friday. We should schedule a pilot kickoff next week.
[21:55] Emily Park: Can we do a live benchmark where you run our sample prompts against dedicated pool?
[22:05] Liam O'Neill: Yes, that's amenable — for Dedicated we can run benchmarks; for hosted we'll simulate with similar model variant. Let's pick a time after we get your prompts.
[22:20] [22:00] Jake Martinez: One last note — how does Redwood surface KV cache hits/misses in traces? Those are critical for our cost analysis.
[22:28] Liam O'Neill: There's a span for cache lookup with attributes hit:true/false and latency. The error analysis groups will show cache miss rates over time.
[22:45] Sara Liu: Ok thanks, this was very helpful.
[22:50] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and the export link.
[23:00] [meeting end]

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcription with occasional mis-heard words (e.g., "gptx-1" transcribed as "gpt ex one"); speaker labels are mostly accurate though sometimes system labeled as generic "Speaker 3" in the raw export.
questions: How to redact PII in prompts?
Can we schedule automated ndjson exports for error types?
How can Redwood integrate traces with our ELK?
